extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and comedic performers (live theatre and television)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for creating, performing, packaging, and teaching improvised comedy (particularly long-form and television adaptations), including format selection, ensemble practice, TV-specific constraints, musical improv, and pedagogical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monologue staging rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of “monologue” is very broad — we just insist that there only be one improviser on stage at any one time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied as a simple production rule limiting stage participants for a monologue; typical cast sizes (e.g., five players) may still play multiple principal and other characters, but only one improviser should occupy the monologue space at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus main characters in a single story
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim is to involve the five main characters in one story, possibly with one or more subplots, and to avoid the effect that new stories can begin at any time, even five minutes before the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the central narrative coherent across the cast; prevent late-starting, unrelated stories (the 'Andy' effect) that undermine dramatic closure and audience satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose format to exploit performers' strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers need to discover what the medium can do for them, and pick the format which will exploit their talents to the fullest, never forgetting to ask the question 'Would this be better if it were scripted?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select short form vs long form, theatrical vs TV packaging, or genre-specific formats (musical, opera, Shakespeare, etc.) based on the cast's skills; be pragmatic and avoid formats that mask weakness or fail the performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve risk and spontaneity on television
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly, the medium of improvisation is wounded once cameras enter the picture. As soon as the audience knows that mistakes could have been edited out, a lot of the risk evaporates, and risk is a primary reason for an audience to see an improvised show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible preserve genuine risk (e.g., live broadcasts) or design TV formats that retain a sense of danger. Recognize that editing/production can sap perceived spontaneity; consider alternatives (live recording, packaging) to keep stakes high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use improvisation differently for TV (behind-the-scenes vs on-camera)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation on TV can be used behind the scenes to generate naturalistic acting style or material (e.g., Curb Your Enthusiasm), or it can be showcased on-camera; the role of improvisation must suit the production's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvisation is a rehearsal tool, capture the script and then perform it tightly on camera. If improvisation is an on-camera feature, accept constraints (editing, format) and design plots/simple lines to allow conversational improv; be explicit about how much improv appears on screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid/scripted-plot approach for TV comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripts for some TV shows include all the details of the plot but omit dialogue, allowing improvisation to provide naturalistic acting while the plot remains structured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing this hybrid approach ensure the plot is well-defined so actors can improvise dialogue without losing narrative coherence; expect substantial editing to shape the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Package televised improv to retain scenework
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone hoping to get a 'pure' improvised show on TV has to do something more than point a camera at their cast and get suggestions from the audience; the bar has been raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design TV formats (e.g., Thank God You're Here) that package the improvisers' challenge, use studio resources intelligently, and preserve elements of theatrical scenework rather than simply broadcasting stage games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on easy laughs and shtick
rubrics_metrics.description: Most theatrical improvisers would look in horror at the easy laughs, lazy shtick and scene-killing gags which paraded across their television screens on a Thursday night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value scene play, character work and storytelling over cheap jokes. While TV audiences may enjoy easy laughs, theatrical standards prioritize craft and depth; be mindful of the different expectations of different media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance ensemble stability and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Having four people working together every week also had advantages: over time a relaxed, mischievous atmosphere began to pervade the show, as running jokes developed between the performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stable troupe builds chemistry and recurring humour, but too-limited casting and repetitive games risk sameness; balance regulars with rotating performers or fresh games to maintain freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge improv on craft, not just audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the audience shouted 'Justification!'... I always knew why a crowd-pleaser shouldn't necessarily be a point-getter. 'Gags' were always looked down upon in after-show notes in a rather snooty way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring/evaluation should reward play quality, justification, story development and technique rather than mere crowd-pleasing stunts; judges/teachers must resist equating laughs per minute with scene quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide structure/genre in advance if appropriate (X-Improvised)
rubrics_metrics.description: As well as structure, many improvised comedy formats involve pre-show decisions about content, or at least premise. In DreamDate, we know we are going to improvise a romantic comedy... and we know it will end with a kiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-defining genre, endpoints, or structural beats can help guide performers in long-form work; this is especially useful when aiming for a coherent story arc rather than an unstructured series of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid genre pastiche unless the cast is inspired
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvised farce, an improvised Christmas pantomime or (god help us) an improvised CSI: Miami is likely simply to be a poorly plotted version of its scripted progenitor with less tight dialogue and no TV wizardry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only attempt X-Improvised (improvised versions of well-known scripted genres) if the cast will be genuinely inspired by the world and capable of elevated improvisation; otherwise it's likely to disappoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do improvised singing only if you're skilled
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people have a complete aversion to almost any kind of improvised singing because, unless you're as good at it as Josie Lawrence... it can be just painful to watch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvised singing requires rapid planning of clever rhymes; if performers lack this skill either avoid improvised musicals or train with a talented musical improviser and take singing lessons before presenting to an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher takes responsibility for student progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Patti took the weight of responsibility from us and told us it was her job to teach, not ours to learn... This is one reason that Tom and I are so emphatic... that the teacher should take the responsibility for the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an empathetic, patient teaching style; diagnose why exercises fail and adapt pedagogy rather than blaming students. Systematically progress from scene beginnings to middles and finally endings, spending time to analyze and train each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze performances to learn why scenes succeed or crash
rubrics_metrics.description: I could suddenly see why improvisers with years more experience than me were struggling or succeeding. I knew when and why scenes or games were crashing and burning, who was rescuing them and who was driving them into a wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly watch and critically analyze shows and rehearsals to identify rescuers, crash causes, timing issues and successful tactics; use these insights to inform teaching, casting and rehearsal focus.
